q: בת 85 אובחנה כסובלת מ- Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR). מה נכון בנוגע למחלה זו?
o: התסמונת שכיחה יותר אצל נשים ביחס של 2:1
70% מחולי PMR הם בגיל מעל 60
כאבים בחגורת אגן יותר שכיחים מאשר כאבים בחגורת כתפיים
ב- 40% מהחולים יש ארטריטיס ארוזיבי של מפרקי כפות הידיים
explanation:
Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) causes aching and morning stiffness in the shoulder and hip girdles after age 50. **Women are affected about twice as often as men.**

**A. Twice as frequent in women** — The female-to-male ratio is about two to one, consistent with the presentation in this 85-year-old woman.
**B. 70% over age 60** — The age distribution is more concentrated in later life. About 90% of cases occur after 60.
**C. Hip pain more frequent** — Shoulder symptoms occur in roughly 75–90% of patients and hip symptoms in 50–70%.
**D. Erosive hand arthritis in 40%** — Peripheral synovitis can involve the hands and wrists, but is usually mild and nonerosive. Erosions warrant evaluation for rheumatoid arthritis.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1600–1601.

q: An older woman with long-standing hypertension develops dizziness when her blood pressure falls abruptly after a treatment change. Why can cerebral ischemic symptoms occur even within a blood pressure range considered normal?
o: The cerebral autoregulatory threshold shifts toward lower pressures
The cerebral autoregulatory threshold shifts toward higher pressures
The abrupt pressure fall increases cerebral blood flow
Acute antihypertensive administration protects against postural hypotension
explanation:
Cerebral autoregulation keeps brain blood flow relatively stable as arterial pressure varies. **Long-standing hypertension can shift the lower limit of autoregulation to higher pressures**, so a rapid fall can cause hypoperfusion before the measured pressure looks unusually low.

**A. Shift to lower pressures** — This would extend tolerance of a pressure fall, contrary to the symptoms.
**B. Shift to higher pressures** — The cerebral vessels can exhaust their capacity to dilate at a higher arterial pressure than expected.
**C. Increased cerebral flow** — Lightheadedness during the abrupt fall is consistent with a transient reduction in flow.
**D. Protection from an acute antihypertensive dose** — A rapid reduction in pressure can provoke symptoms. Gradual long-term hypertension control has different effects.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 668.

q: גבר בן 78 מגיע לחדר מיון לאחר 2.5 שעות מתחילת חולשה פתאומית בצד ימין ובעיות בדיבור. NIHSS 12, לא נוטל אנטיקואגולנטים. CT ראש ללא דימום. מה ההמלצה לגבי טיפול תרומבוליטי?
o: לא לתת rt-PA בגלל גיל מתקדם מעל 75
לתת rt-PA אם אין התוויות נגד אחרות
לדחות החלטה עד ביצוע MRI
לתת אספירין בלבד בגלל הגיל
explanation:
חולשה פתאומית והפרעת דיבור שנותרו לאחר שעתיים וחצי הן חסר משמעותי בחלון שבו ניתן להציל רקמת מוח. **יש לתת תרומבוליזה תוך־ורידית אם המטופל מתאים לאחר השלמת הבדיקה הדחופה**.

**א. להימנע מעל גיל 75** גיל 78 כשלעצמו אינו התוויית נגד, וגם מטופלים מבוגרים יותר עשויים להפיק תועלת.
**ב. לתת כשאין התוויות נגד נוספות** CT ללא דימום, חסר משמעותי וזמן התחלה ידוע תומכים בטיפול. משלימים במהירות בדיקת לחץ דם, תרופות וסיכוני דמם.
**ג. להמתין ל־MRI** CT ללא חומר ניגוד מאפשר לשלול דימום. אין צורך לעכב טיפול מתאים לשם הוכחת האוטם ב־MRI.
**ד. לתת אספירין בלבד** אספירין משמש למניעה במצבים מתאימים, אך גיל לבדו אינו סיבה לוותר על טיפול לפתיחת העורק.

q: A 78-year-old woman with diabetes and mild cognitive impairment is brought by her daughter because of vulvar discomfort. She has difficulty describing her symptoms. Examination shows erythematous plaques without the silvery appearance typical of her psoriasis on the elbows and knees. Which diagnosis best matches this genital appearance?
o: Vulvar lichen sclerosus
Genital psoriatic lesions
Erosive lichen planus
Genital herpes simplex
explanation:
Genital psoriasis can appear red and lack the familiar silvery scale seen on extensor surfaces. **Erythematous vulvar plaques in a woman with established psoriasis** fit genital involvement.

**A. Lichen sclerosus.** Porcelain-white plaques, purpura and architectural change are more characteristic.
**B. Genital psoriasis.** Moist genital skin may show little scale despite typical scaly plaques elsewhere.
**C. Erosive lichen planus.** Painful erosions, discharge and labial scarring suggest a different inflammatory disorder.
**D. Genital herpes.** Painful vesicles or ulcers are more typical than persistent psoriatic plaques.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 532.

. Genital herpes.** Painful vesicles or ulcers are more typical than persistent psoriatic plaques.

q: A community-based trial in older patients with advanced cancer found an absolute reduction of 20% in treatment toxicity with comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA)-guided interventions. Which description captures the approach described by Hazzard?
o: It uses routine history and examination as the assessment for age-related problems and intervention planning
It forwards an assessment report to the oncologist while retaining the usual treatment pathway
It identifies missed aging-related problems and directs interventions tailored to the findings
It centers assessment on tumor characteristics while leaving functional assessment to the usual pathway
explanation:
In GAP70+, community oncologists received a summary of age-related impairments and tailored management recommendations. **Using those findings to guide care lowered three-month grade 3–5 toxicity from 71% to 51%.**

**A. Routine history and examination** — Usual assessment can miss falls, nutritional difficulties or a need for help with daily activities.
**B. Forward a report and retain usual care** — The intervention gave oncologists specific management recommendations, beyond merely forwarding findings.
**C. Identify problems and tailor interventions** — A deficit could prompt a medication change, a fall-prevention measure or discussion of treatment intensity. The observed absolute difference was about 20 percentage points.
**D. Center assessment on the tumor** — Tumor characteristics guide drug selection but do not reveal functional risks that can be addressed during treatment.

Reference · GAP70+, Lancet 2021, pp. 1894–1904 (PMID 34741815) · Hazzard 8e, p. 1388.
ref: Hazzard Ch 88 — CANCER AND AGING: GENERAL PRINCIPLES

. Forward a report and retain usual care** — The intervention gave oncologists specific management recommendations, beyond merely forwarding findings.

. Identify problems and tailor interventions** — A deficit could prompt a medication change, a fall-prevention measure or discussion of treatment intensity. The observed absolute difference was about 20 percentage points.
. Center assessment on the tumor** — Tumor characteristics guide drug selection but do not reveal functional risks that can be addressed during treatment.

q: An older woman with recurrent falls takes amitriptyline for neuropathic pain. Which adverse-effect profile supports reassessing this medicine under the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria?
o: Anticholinergic effects with sedation and orthostatic hypotension
Anticholinergic effects with alertness and improved postural stability
Sedative effects with protection against orthostatic blood-pressure changes
Antidepressant effects with alertness and improved postural stability
explanation:
Amitriptyline can relieve neuropathic pain but has substantial anticholinergic and cardiovascular effects. **Sedation and orthostatic hypotension add to its anticholinergic burden.**

**A. Anticholinergic, sedating and hypotensive** — Together these effects can impair attention and stability during the transition to standing.
**B. Anticholinergic but alert and stable** — Its anticholinergic activity is real. The proposed improvement in alertness and stability is inconsistent with its sedating effects.
**C. Sedating but protects standing pressure** — The sedation is plausible, while the claimed protection is reversed. The drug can produce orthostatic hypotension.
**D. Antidepressant and stabilizing** — An antidepressant indication describes therapeutic use and does not eliminate this tricyclic drug's adverse effects.

Reference · 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, Table 2, p. 2059.

. Antidepressant and stabilizing** — An antidepressant indication describes therapeutic use and does not eliminate this tricyclic drug's adverse effects.

q: A man receiving chronic benzodiazepine treatment develops delirium after the medication is stopped around surgery. Evaluation establishes a withdrawal syndrome. How does this cause affect the role of benzodiazepines?
o: They are primarily indicated to improve orientation in dementia
They are primarily indicated for delirium caused by infection
They are the treatment of choice for withdrawal-related delirium
They are the treatment of choice for delirium caused by hypoxia
explanation:
Abrupt discontinuation of a regularly taken benzodiazepine can cause withdrawal delirium. Here the drug treats the withdrawal mechanism.
**A benzodiazepine is the treatment of choice for established withdrawal-related delirium, followed by a carefully managed taper when appropriate.**

**A. They are primarily indicated to improve orientation in dementia.** It does not restore orientation in dementia.
**B. They are primarily indicated for delirium caused by infection.** In infection-related delirium, treat the infection and avoid unnecessary sedation.
**C. They are the treatment of choice for withdrawal-related delirium.** Treating withdrawal addresses the precipitant rather than simply suppressing behavior.
**D. They are the treatment of choice for delirium caused by hypoxia.** In hypoxic delirium, restore oxygenation and assess its cause. Sedation can impair respiratory monitoring.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 885, 889

q: בן 82 בישראל התאושש מאצירת שתן ומזיהום. מוצע ניתוח TURP שאינו דחוף. הוא מסוגל להבין את המידע ואומר שמטרתו נוחות. טרם נמסר לו הסבר על תועלת, סיכונים וחלופות. מהו הצעד הנדרש לפני החלטה?
o: לקבל את ההחלטה על סמך המלצת האורולוג.
להסביר תועלת, סיכונים וחלופות ולברר את בחירתו.
להעדיף את החלופה הנוחה יותר למשפחה.
לבחור לפי שיעור ההצלחה הטכנית של הניתוח.
explanation:
**יש להסביר תועלת, סיכונים וחלופות ל־TURP ולקבל את בחירתו.** במקרה זה חשוב לקשור את ההסבר למטרתו המוצהרת, נוחות.

**א. לקבל את ההחלטה על סמך המלצת האורולוג** — המלצה מקצועית היא מרכיב בדיון ולא הסכמה מטעם המטופל.
**ב. להסביר תועלת, סיכונים וחלופות ולברר את בחירתו** — יש לכלול גם את המשמעות של המשך טיפול שמרני או בצנתר.
**ג. להעדיף את החלופה הנוחה יותר למשפחה** — נטל הטיפול בבית רלוונטי, אך אינו גובר על בחירתו.
**ד. לבחור לפי שיעור ההצלחה הטכנית של הניתוח** — אינה מתארת תסמינים, סיבוכים ואיכות חיים לאחר הניתוח.

אסמכתא · חוק זכויות החולה, סעיף 13.

q: A 78-year-old woman living alone in a two-story home has fallen three times in two weeks. She says she simply tripped. MMSE is 28/30, gait speed 0.7 m/s, tandem walking is impaired, and Romberg testing is positive. Vision is 20/40 in both eyes with cataracts. She takes hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg and atorvastatin 40 mg. Vitamin B12 is 180 pg/mL (laboratory lower limit 200); folate and TSH are normal. Which approach addresses the range of risk factors through a multifactorial falls-prevention plan?
o: Prioritize cataract intervention for the visual deficit.
Prioritize vitamin B12 replacement for the laboratory finding.
Install grab bars to reduce risk in the bathroom.
Coordinate interventions for the patient’s individual fall risks.
explanation:
Slow gait, poor tandem walking, reduced vision and an abnormal Romberg result point to more than a loose stair or a single laboratory value. **Coordinate interventions across her assessed risks.**

**A. Prioritize cataract intervention for the visual deficit** — Improving vision can help, but reduced balance and possible sensory loss still need assessment.
**B. Prioritize vitamin B12 replacement for the laboratory finding** — Low B12 and imbalance merit attention. Replacement will not immediately correct the staircase, visual impairment or slow gait.
**C. Install grab bars to reduce risk in the bathroom** — A home adaptation can reduce environmental demands without correcting the sensory and mobility problems.
**D. Coordinate interventions for the patient’s individual fall risks** — Review medications and orthostasis, clarify sensory loss and B12 status, and address vision, exercise needs and home hazards together.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 635–637, 639–641 and 670.

. Install grab bars to reduce risk in the bathroom** — A home adaptation can reduce environmental demands without correcting the sensory and mobility problems.

q: An 81-year-old man with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction is being considered for an ICD. He recently fell and needs help managing his affairs. Which consideration accurately describes the discussion of implantation in Hazzard?
o: Emphasize the expected ICD benefit in symptom relief and quality of life
Expect ICD benefit to increase with age because overall mortality risk rises
Discuss comorbidity, life expectancy, and goals in shared ICD decision-making
Expect a life expectancy of a few months to strengthen the benefit of implantation
explanation:
An ICD can prevent sudden arrhythmic death but does not relieve congestion. **Discuss functional prognosis, comorbidity and personal goals** because implantation helps less when another illness is likely to determine survival.

**A. Promise symptom relief** A defibrillator treats a dangerous rhythm after it occurs. It does not improve pump function by itself.
**B. Expect benefit to increase with age** Competing causes of death and procedural complications can reduce the net benefit in advanced age.
**C. Use shared decision-making** Include the likelihood of meaningful survival, risk of shocks and the patient's preferences about life prolongation.
**D. Favor implantation with months to live** A short life expectancy leaves little time for primary prevention to improve outcomes. For primary prevention, implantation ordinarily requires an expectation of meaningful survival beyond one year.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1184, 1190. AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline (2022), §7.4.1.

q: An 80-year-old woman with limited mobility cannot safely reach the toilet at night. Constipation treatment and medication review are already underway. Which environmental intervention directly addresses toilet access?
o: Use a bedpan in bed for bowel movements
Provide an accessible commode and help with transfers
Restrict toilet access to predetermined staff-care times
Use a distant toilet without a way to call for assistance
explanation:
An urge to defecate is of little help if a person cannot safely reach a toilet. Postponing evacuation because of the environment can compound retention.
**Provide a safely accessible commode and help with transfers.**

**A. Use a bedpan.** A supported seated posture better facilitates defecation and comfort when attainable.
**B. Accessible commode and assistance.** This reduces the distance and transfer barrier. Provide privacy and a way to call for help.
**C. Restrict access to staff schedules.** The resident needs a way to respond to the urge outside scheduled care times.
**D. Distant toilet without assistance.** This maintains the barrier and increases the risk of an unsafe transfer or fall.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 1371, Table 87-8.

q: What does comprehensive geriatric assessment add to treatment planning for an older woman with breast cancer?
o: Replacing functional assessment with a summary of the history and examination
Identifying functional and cognitive deficits to help guide treatment planning
Choosing treatment by age while reducing the assessment of comorbid disease
Replacing medication review with an assessment of the stage of the tumor
explanation:
Patients with the same tumor stage can differ in mobility, memory, comorbidity, medications and available help. **Comprehensive geriatric assessment finds deficits that can change treatment selection and the support needed to complete treatment.**

**A. Replace assessment of function with a routine history** — Ask explicitly about everyday tasks and mobility. A routine office assessment may miss limitations that matter between treatment visits.
**B. Identify functional and cognitive deficits** — Discovering difficulty walking or managing tablets can prompt rehabilitation, medication support or caregiver involvement before treatment starts.
**C. Select treatment by age** — Age alone cannot distinguish a fit patient from a vulnerable one. Comorbid conditions and their effect on function contribute to expected tolerance and life expectancy.
**D. Replace medication review with tumor staging** — Staging estimates cancer extent. Reviewing prescriptions identifies treatment burden, adverse effects and potential interactions, so it remains part of the assessment.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1401–1402, geriatric screening and comprehensive geriatric assessment.

q: אילו ממצאים צפויים בבדיקת הספירומטריה במבוגרים?
o: FEV1 ( Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 sec ) לא משתנה עם הגיל
TLC ( Total Lung Capacity ) יורד עם הגיל
יחס FEV1/FVC יורד עם הגיל
DLCO ( Diffusing Capacity of Lung for Carbone Monoxide ) לא משתנה עם הגיל
explanation:
Spirometry measures the volume expelled during a forced expiration and how quickly it leaves the lungs. The FEV1/FVC ratio is the fraction of the total forced breath that comes out in the first second.

**The FEV1/FVC ratio tends to fall with age because FEV1 falls proportionately more than FVC.** Interpret an individual's result against an age-appropriate lower limit and the clinical picture.

**A. FEV1 is unchanged.** Less elastic recoil and earlier airway closure reduce first-second emptying.
**B. TLC falls.** Weaker inward lung recoil favors a larger inflated volume while chest-wall stiffness limits expansion. Together these effects leave total lung capacity relatively stable.
**C. FEV1/FVC falls.** When early expiratory emptying declines more than the total volume exhaled, a smaller fraction of the breath leaves in the first second.
**D. DLCO is unchanged.** Gas transfer generally declines with the effective capillary surface. DLCO needs a gas-transfer test and TLC needs a volume measurement beyond simple spirometry.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, Ch 80, pp1230–1231. ERS/ATS technical standard on interpretive strategies for routine lung function tests, Table 1, Eur Respir J 2022;60:2101499.

explanation:
Among these features, prominent **bradykinesia** signals greater risk of cognitive decline in Parkinson disease. Motor phenotype and severity carry more prognostic information than the side of onset.

**A. Young motor onset.** Older age and older onset generally increase dementia risk.
**B. Tremor.** A tremor-dominant phenotype usually carries less cognitive risk than a predominantly akinetic or gait-impaired phenotype.
**C. Bradykinesia.** Marked slowness reflects an akinetic phenotype associated with greater cognitive risk.
**D. Left-sided onset.** Unilateral onset is common in Parkinson disease. The side alone is a weak predictor here.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 985.

q: An older patient with fecal soiling and a weak external sphincter is being considered for biofeedback and sphincter-strengthening exercises after reversible bowel problems have been addressed. Which finding limits the ability to learn and use these exercises?
o: Excessive pelvic floor descent during attempted rectal evacuation
Significant cognitive impairment affecting executive function and memory
Fecal soiling associated with a weak external sphincter
Rectal outlet delay accompanied by persistent excessive straining
explanation:
Biofeedback and sphincter exercises require the patient to understand a task, act on feedback and retain the routine. Simply having the physical symptoms targeted by training does not determine whether training is feasible.
**Significant executive or memory impairment limits the ability to learn and use the exercises.**

**A. Pelvic-floor descent.** This can affect the response to pelvic rehabilitation but does not directly explain failure to remember training.
**B. Cognitive impairment.** Difficulty sequencing and retaining instructions can make independent practice impractical.
**C. Weak external sphincter and soiling.** These are reasons to consider strengthening when participation is feasible.
**D. Straining with outlet delay.** This can be an indication for pelvic-floor retraining.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, pp. 1370–1371.

explanation:
Falling glucose activates autonomic warning symptoms and counterregulatory hormones. Impaired autonomic function narrows the window for recognizing and correcting a low.

**Autonomic nervous system dysfunction increases hypoglycemia risk.** Reduced glucagon or growth-hormone responses can compound this loss of protection.

**A. Greater glucagon secretion.** Glucagon supports hepatic glucose release. A reduced response is the risk.
**B. Greater beta-adrenergic receptor function.** Weaker adrenergic signaling compromises warning and defense.
**C. Greater growth-hormone response.** The response to hypoglycemia tends to be blunted with aging.
**D. Autonomic dysfunction.** Fewer warning symptoms and impaired counterregulation permit a low to progress unnoticed.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p1584, Table 99-15.

q: What clinical clue (hallucination type + cognitive screen result) is highly suggestive of DLB rather than AD?
o: Visual hallucinations first appearing with severe global impairment.
Isolated failure of delayed recall with preserved perception.
Auditory hallucinations with relatively preserved MMSE.
Visual hallucinations with an MMSE above 20.
explanation:
Dementia with Lewy bodies often produces well-formed visual hallucinations early. **Visual hallucinations while the MMSE is still above 20** favor this diagnosis over typical Alzheimer disease.

**A. Visual hallucinations first appearing with severe global impairment** — Waiting for advanced cognitive decline misses an early diagnostic clue.
**B. Isolated failure of delayed recall with preserved perception** — Prominent amnestic impairment more strongly suggests a typical Alzheimer presentation.
**C. Auditory hallucinations with relatively preserved MMSE** — These do not carry the same diagnostic weight as recurrent visual hallucinations.
**D. Visual hallucinations with an MMSE above 20** — The combination is particularly suggestive when accompanied by parkinsonism or fluctuations.

Reference · Hazzard 8e, p. 871.

FUROSAMIDE
ENALAPRIL
MILIRONE
keySource: IMA 2025-Jun Basic official answer key after appeals, Q128
chapterTitle: Harrison 22e ch. 316 – Cardiogenic Shock and Pulmonary Edema
explanation:
Improving congestion or cardiac output is different from directly increasing myocardial contractility. **Milrinone is the direct positive inotrope** among these drugs. The others can ease cardiac loading conditions without strengthening contraction directly.

**A. Nitroglycerin.** Venodilation reduces preload, often relieving pulmonary congestion.
**B. Furosemide.** Diuresis reduces excess volume and filling pressure.
**C. Enalapril.** ACE inhibition reduces afterload and neurohormonal stress.
**D. Milrinone.** Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibition increases contractility and also produces vasodilation.

Reference · Harrison 22e, p. 2331.
Key note: The exam accepted all four agents. Harrison distinguishes relief of congestion or unloading from direct positive inotropy, which only milrinone provides among these options.

explanation:
Nitrates lower preload by venodilation. **Avoid them in right ventricular infarction** because a preload-dependent right ventricle may not sustain output after venous return falls.

**A. Mild aortic stenosis.** Severe aortic stenosis is the stronger concern. Mild stenosis alone is not the specific contraindication tested here.
**B. Lateral-wall infarction.** A lateral infarct location alone does not create the same preload dependence.
**C. Pulmonary edema.** Nitrates may relieve hypertensive pulmonary congestion if blood pressure permits.
**D. Right ventricular infarction.** A sudden fall in preload can cause profound hypotension in right ventricular infarction.

Reference · Harrison 22e, p. 2109.
